question: A 57-year-old patient diagnosed with stage T3N1M0 colon adenocarcinoma. He was treated with resection followed by postoperative FOLFOX chemotherapy (fluorouracil, leucovorin and oxaliplatin) for six months. In a routine control, two years later, elevation of carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) was detected at 30 ng / mL (previous to less than 2 ng / mL). He has no symptoms, the physical examination is bland, the chest radiograph is normal. On CT, a mass of 3 cm is seen in the right hepatic lobe, which is captured in PET. No other alterations were observed in CT or PET. What attitude seems more correct?

options.opa: Chemotherapy with FOLFIRI (fluorouracil, leucovorin and irinotecan) plus bevacizumab.
options.opc: Evaluation by resection surgery of the hepatic lesion.

enhanced_information: Elevated CEA (30 ng/mL) suggests possible cancer recurrence, confirmed by a 3 cm hepatic mass on CT and PET uptake, indicating active tumor cells. Given isolated liver disease, surgical resection offers a chance for cure. Chemotherapy with FOLFIRI plus bevacizumab is a standard treatment for metastatic colorectal cancer and may improve outcomes. Evaluation for resection surgery of the hepatic lesion is a potentially curative option with a chance for long-term survival.
analysis: The core medical principle here is to consider the possibility of cancer recurrence in a patient with elevated CEA and a hepatic lesion on imaging. Given the isolated liver disease and the potential for cure, the most appropriate approach would be to consider resection surgery of the hepatic lesion. This offers a chance for long-term survival and potentially curative outcomes.
